rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to observe all 10 compounds and locate the elution window while keeping the run near the 10-minute scoring target. The intermediate temperature leaves room to tune selectivity in either direction.

Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the crowded central pairs respond to slope. The initial last peak at 7.16 minutes leaves room to improve resolution without exceeding the 10-minute scoring threshold.

The critical pair improved markedly with a shallower gradient, so reduce the slope further. Raising the starting organic fraction trims the weak-solvent segment to help keep the last peak within 10 minutes while retaining the first peak.

Injection 3 reached the maximum CRF. Shift the gradient window upward while preserving its 0.05-per-minute slope to test a shorter fully resolved separation; retain injection 3 as the established best method.

Change only temperature to test whether selectivity can resolve the remaining close pair in the shorter method. Injection 3 already secures the maximum CRF, so this explores a faster fully resolved alternative.

Test a modest temperature decrease from injection 4 to shift the crowded middle peaks in the opposite direction. This may restore full resolution while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes; injection 3 remains the proven maximum-score method.

Return to 40 C and lengthen injection 4’s gradient to improve its single under-resolved pair. The slope response seen earlier suggests this could achieve full resolution while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

With the maximum CRF already secured, explore a faster high-temperature separation that may move the central peaks beyond their selectivity crossover. Lowering phi0 relative to recent runs protects early-peak retention while the shorter gradient reduces elution time.

Lengthen only the high-temperature gradient to determine whether its sole under-resolved pair responds to slope. The last peak at 6.61 minutes leaves substantial room to gain resolution without a time penalty.

At 60 C, lengthening the gradient worsened the limiting pair, so test a substantially steeper gradient instead. This may separate that pair while retaining adequate resolution elsewhere and shortening the run.

Test an intermediate temperature with a steeper gradient to balance the competing central-pair separations seen at 40 and 60 C. The lower starting organic fraction protects early-peak resolution while targeting a faster alternative to the established maximum-score method.

Test 55 C to shift the limiting central pair away from its near-coelution at 50 C. A lower starting organic fraction also changes central selectivity and preserves early retention, while targeting a fully resolved run shorter than the established optimum.

Test a shallower gradient at 55 C, where temperature has already improved separation of the later central pair. The neighboring pair appears near an elution-order crossover, so this tests whether the slope change separates both pairs while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.
Lengthen injection 13’s gradient slightly to lift its sole marginal pair from R = 1.41 above 1.5. The last peak at 8.54 minutes leaves room for this adjustment without a time penalty.

Shift the starting organic fraction upward while keeping nearly the same slope as injection 14 to shorten the fully resolved separation. Check both the central pairs and the early pair, which may lose resolution at the stronger starting solvent.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve the central pair that deteriorated in injection 15, while shortening the gradient relative to injection 14. This tests whether the weaker start permits full resolution at an earlier last-peak time.

Slightly steepen injection 16’s gradient to shorten the fastest fully resolved method found so far. The predicted last-peak elution composition remains well below 0.85, and the small slope change should preserve resolution of both critical pairs.

Increase the slope slightly from 0.0625 to 0.065 organic fraction per minute to shorten injection 17 while targeting full resolution. The last peak should still elute within the gradient, and the observed slope response predicts the critical pairs will remain above R = 1.5.

Test whether a weaker starting solvent improves central selectivity enough to permit a steeper, faster gradient. Injection 18 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method; this run checks a new route to shortening it.
Slightly reduce injection 19’s gradient slope to lift its limiting pair above R = 1.5. This targets full resolution with the last peak around 7.6 minutes, potentially faster than injection 18.

With maximum CRF secured, explore the untested low-temperature selectivity regime for a faster fully resolved alternative. The stronger starting solvent and shorter gradient should offset some increased retention; injection 20 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Preserve injection 20’s successful 0.075-per-minute slope while ending the gradient earlier at 0.65, above the last peak’s estimated elution composition of 0.57. This should retain maximum CRF and the 7.60-minute separation with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a small slope increase from injection 18 to probe the boundary of full resolution and potentially shorten its 7.76-minute separation. The central pair at R = 1.55 is the main risk; injection 22 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Preserve the proven 0.075-per-minute slope and starting composition of injections 20 and 22, while testing a higher final organic fraction for stronger post-elution washing. All peaks should retain their demonstrated resolution and 7.60-minute last-peak time, maintaining maximum CRF.

Preserve the proven gradient slope through all closely spaced peaks, then test a lower-organic hold for the isolated last compound. This explores a reduced-solvent maximum-score method; injections 20 and 22 remain the fastest confirmed fully resolved options.
